# Expressions

<a id="expressions-truthy-positions"></a>

## Six syntax positions test truthiness; every other `bool` position stays checked

`rule:expressions/truthy-positions`

Exactly six syntax positions test a value's truthiness instead of requiring it to already be `bool`:
`if`/`elseif`'s condition, `while`/`do…while`'s condition, `for`'s middle clause, the ternary and
elvis condition, and the operands of `&&`, `||` and `!`. Each accepts a value of **any** type —
`mixed`, a union, a scalar, an array, an object, an enum case, `callable` — with no diagnostic for
not already being `bool`, and answers by [`expressions/truthy-table`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-table).

The list is closed and nothing narrower gets the exception. Assigning into a `bool`-typed parameter,
property, return or local still needs an explicit `as bool` or a comparison; `==` and `match` still
compare rather than test ([`expressions/switch-match-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-switch-match-equality)); `??` and `?->` test null against
not-null, which is a different axis and untouched.

A truthiness test converts nothing. It produces no value of a different type that can be read back,
assigned or passed on — it answers "branch or don't", freshly, every time — so a declared type never
changes here.

That is why the exception costs no safety. What a checked conversion protects against is a declared
type changing silently, and a condition changes none. Without it, every "is this set" test — `if
($rows)`, `while ($line)`, `$user && $user->active`, `!$items` — would need `!= ''`, a count or an
`as bool` at every branch. The cost is one question to hold while reading a condition: whether this
position is one of the six. The list is short, fixed and syntactically obvious.

**Declined:**
- **No truthiness anywhere, so every condition must already be `bool`.** It puts the ceremony back at
  every branch, and safety does not need it.
- **Truthiness for `null` and `bool` only, with other scalars needing `as bool`.** It draws a line
  inside the table with no principled edge: `if ($rows)` is as common as `if ($maybeNull)`.
- **Truthiness in `if`, `while` and the ternary, but `bool` operands for `&&`, `||` and `!`.** The
  same value would be bare in one place and refused two tokens later, and `$user && $user->active`
  is as common as a bare `if`.

<sub>See also [`expressions/truthy-table`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-table), [`expressions/nullable-condition-lint`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-condition-lint), [`expressions/no-keyword-logical-operators`](expressions.md#expressions-no-keyword-logical-operators), [`iteration/for-init-clause`](iteration.md#iteration-for-init-clause).</sub>

<a id="expressions-truthy-table"></a>

## The truthy table is PHP's, and `bytes` is falsy only when it is empty

`rule:expressions/truthy-table`

A condition is decided by one truthy table over Novis's type set:

| type | falsy | truthy |
|---|---|---|
| `null` | always | never |
| `bool` | `false` | `true` |
| `int` / `uint` | `0` | anything else |
| `float` | `0.0`, including `-0.0`; `NAN` is truthy | anything else |
| `string` | `""` and the one-character `"0"` | every other string, `"0.0"` and `"false"` included |
| `bytes` | empty, and **only** empty | every non-empty buffer, the one-octet `"0"` included |
| `array<T>` | empty, for any `T` | one or more elements, whatever they hold |
| class instance, `callable` | never | always |
| enum case | never | always ([`enums/truthiness`](enums.md#enums-truthiness)) |
| `mixed`, a union | dispatched on the runtime tag, one row per tag | — |

**The `bytes` row drops the `"0"` case deliberately.** That exception belongs to text that may be read
as a number, and `bytes` is the type that never converts to one. A `bytes` reaching a condition through
a `mixed` takes the same row, so the two
spellings of one buffer never disagree.

Where the static type is a scalar, array, class, `callable` or enum, the compiler knows the row and
lowers to the matching native test with no dispatch. Only a `mixed` or union condition pays for a
runtime helper.

The table's own surprises are kept with it: `"0"` is falsy while `"0.0"` and `"false"` are truthy,
and an array of falsy elements is truthy. Code review, not the compiler, catches a condition that
meant something else. A ported program that treats `"0.0"` as falsy has a bug of its own, since
PHP never did either.

<sub>See also [`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions), [`enums/truthiness`](enums.md#enums-truthiness), [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics).</sub>

<a id="expressions-no-keyword-logical-operators"></a>

## `and`, `or` and `xor` do not parse, and `&&`/`||` are the whole set

`rule:expressions/no-keyword-logical-operators`

`and`, `or` and `xor` are rejected at parse time, in every position, as `E0226`. Each keyword is
still recognised where an infix logical operator would go, so the diagnostic can name the fix, but
the expression becomes an error node: there is no low-precedence AND or OR in the tree at all.

`&&` and `||` are the only logical connectives, at every precedence, and `!` is untouched. The
diagnostic for `and` and `or` names the one-token replacement.

`xor` has none. There is no `^^` operator, so its diagnostic names the two rewrites instead —
`(a || b) && !(a && b)` for the general truthy case, or `a != b` when both operands are already
`bool`. That is a real, narrow capability subtraction rather than a spelling change.

All three keywords stay reserved words. They are not freed for use as identifiers, which is what lets
the diagnostic fire at all. A chain such as `$a and $b or $c` reports once per keyword: each keyword
consumes its own right-hand operand, so the error does not cascade into unrelated token errors.

The word forms are not synonyms for `&&` and `||`: they bind looser than `=`, so `$x = $a and $b`
assigns `$a` and discards `$b`. That precedence gap is a trap with nothing on the other side of the
scale, and keeping a second spelling of each connective is what [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)
rules out everywhere else. Compatibility is with what a PHP program observably does, not with every
way PHP lets it be written.

**Declined:**
- **The keywords with PHP's precedence.** It would take a second short-circuit lowering at a third
  precedence tier, built and tested only to reproduce the trap above.
- **`and` and `or` as plain aliases of `&&` and `||`, dropping only `xor`.** A second spelling buys
  nothing once the meaning matches, the same reason [`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast) gives for `(int)$x`.
- **A deprecation warning first, removal later.** A refused PHP spelling is a hard error with no
  warning tier, as [`core-api/casing-has-no-suppression`](core-api.md#core-api-casing-has-no-suppression) reasons.

<sub>See also [`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions), [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator).</sub>

<a id="expressions-nullable-condition-lint"></a>

## A `?T` used directly as a condition is warned about, not refused

`rule:expressions/nullable-condition-lint`

`nvs check` warns with `W1023` when a condition's type is a union with `null` in it, naming `!= null`
as the fix. `?bool` warns too, since `null` and `false` are both false. A bare `null` and `mixed` do
not warn. Every position `check_condition` (`crates/nvs-types/src/expr/mod.rs`) covers raises it:
`if`, `while`, `do`/`while`, a `for` header's middle clause and a ternary's condition.

Both `null` and `0` are falsy, so `if ($s as ?int)` is false for an invalid value *and* for a valid
zero — reconstructing precisely the `(int)$x > 0` defect that nullable conversion exists to remove.

It is a warning and not a diagnostic because **the hazard is not new and not specific to the
operator**: any `?int` in an `if` has always had it. Refusing it would narrow
[`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions) for every nullable value in the language, which is a larger change
than this one.

**Declined:**
- **Refusing a `?T` condition outright.** It is the strongest guard against the trap, but it changes
  [`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions) for every nullable value rather than for conversions.
- **Warning only where the non-`null` half has a falsy value.** A `?User` cannot be confused with a
  falsy object, but one rule for every `?T` is simpler to learn, and `!= null` reads the same for
  each.

<sub>See also [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion), [`expressions/truthy-table`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-table), [`expressions/bare-throwable-arm-warns`](expressions.md#expressions-bare-throwable-arm-warns).</sub>

<a id="expressions-misread-grouping-warns"></a>

## Two operator mixes whose grouping a reader misreads warn with `W1022`, offering the parentheses that keep the meaning and the grouping most likely meant

`rule:expressions/misread-grouping-warns`

`nvs check` warns with `W1022` at two operator mixes whose grouping a reader misreads, and at no others:
a `??` whose right operand is an arithmetic or `.` expression written without parentheses
(`$n ?? 0 + 10` is `$n ?? (0 + 10)`), and a `?:`, long or short, whose condition is one of those or a
`??` (`"n=" . $ok ? "x" : "y"` tests `"n=" . $ok`, so it is always `"x"`).

The list is closed because every shape on it is valid code, and a warning on valid code is worth its
noise only where the misreading is common. `&&` beside `||`, `-2 ** 2` and a nested ternary are left
alone: the first is common, deliberate and well understood, the second is pinned by the reference's
own precedence table, and the third groups to the right as documented. A parenthesized operand never
warns. Neither shape is a type error, which is why nothing else reports it: `??` binds looser than
every arithmetic operator and `.`, and a ternary condition accepts any type and tests its truthiness
([`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions)).

The grammar is unchanged, so the warning costs nothing when the program runs. The parser raises it,
seeing each written operator once with its source at hand: one `match` per `??`, per `?:` and per
invalid assignment target, allocating only when it warns, and nothing is held past the diagnostic.

Each warning carries two edits. Parentheses around what the code does now change nothing, so
`source.fixAll.nvs` may apply them on save. The grouping the author most likely meant, the `??` or `?`
taking the operand nearest it, changes what the line does, so it is an alternative a person picks from
the light bulb and no batch applies ([`ide/a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion`](ide.md#ide-a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion)).

Two errors name the same kind of parentheses. `E0105` on `$ok && $row = $next` offers the grouping
`$ok && ($row = $next)` and recovers the parse as it, so no second error follows
about a target nobody meant. `E0706` on `$flags & 4 == 4`, which is `$flags & (4 == 4)`, offers
`($flags & 4) == 4`, with a help line about precedence in place of its general one about converting
the operand. Each of these two fixes is the only grouping of its line that compiles, so neither is an
alternative. Both errors keep their codes and messages.

**Declined:**

- **An error for the warned shapes.** Each is valid code with one meaning, and refusing it would
  break programs that meant exactly that meaning.
- **A hint in the editor alone.** `nvs check` and CI would never see it, and the language server would
  carry a second copy of a check the compiler makes once.

<sub>See also [`ide/a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion`](ide.md#ide-a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion), [`expressions/nullable-condition-lint`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-condition-lint), [`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions), [`expressions/catch-expression-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression-precedence).</sub>

<a id="expressions-one-equality-operator"></a>

## `==` and `!=` are the whole of equality, and `===`, `!==` and `<>` do not parse

`rule:expressions/one-equality-operator`

There is **one** equality operator, `==`, and its negation `!=`. `===` and `!==` do not parse
(`E0232`); `<>` does not parse either (`E0241`), and each diagnostic names the edit. There is no
suppression and no dialect flag: a construct that parses in one project and not another is two
languages.

`!=` is exactly `!( … == … )`. There is no third relation.

Nothing for a second spelling to distinguish survives, because there is no loose comparison to escape
from. `==` never converts either operand; both operands must be able to hold the same value
([`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused)); each type's answer is the strict one
([`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics)), objects compare by identity
([`expressions/object-identity-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-object-identity-equality)), and only a `mixed` or union pairing is decided at run
time ([`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality)).

Ordering — `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `<=>` — is a separate question with its own rule, and this operator
says nothing about it.

Loose comparison is a hazard family, not a convenience: a falsy value passing a loose test is why
verification returns claims or throws ([`security/verification-throws-and-compares-in-constant-time`](security.md#security-verification-throws-and-compares-in-constant-time)). Removing the
construct closes the family, and security and request isolation are not traded for familiarity. The
standard library already compares strictly: `Core\Arr::contains` is always strict, and the natural
ordering throws on a pair from two different rows rather than converting one side. One operator keeps
the library and the language on one answer. `==` is also the spelling of every language without
juggling, so a reader arriving from anywhere but PHP already knows it.

The porting cost is real and lands mostly on one row: `"1" == "01"` is true in PHP and false here, and
nothing in the compiled program flags it. A defensive `$x == null` on a non-nullable type, copied from
PHP, stops compiling; the check was always dead.

**Declined:**
- **Both operators, with PHP's meanings.** That brings the loose-comparison hazard family back, and with
  this type system the two spellings would disagree only on the three rows nobody chooses the loose
  reading for.
- **Both operators, with `==` defined as strict.** Two spellings for one operation
  ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)), and the worse one: a PHP reader seeing `==` assumes
  juggling that is not there.
- **`===` kept and `==` dropped.** `===` exists only as an escape from a loose `==`. With nothing to
  escape, it is three characters saying what two say everywhere else.

<sub>See also [`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused), [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics), [`expressions/object-identity-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-object-identity-equality), [`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality), [`expressions/switch-match-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-switch-match-equality).</sub>

<a id="expressions-equality-semantics"></a>

## Equality has one row per type, and every row is the strict reading

`rule:expressions/equality-semantics`

Nothing converts. Each type has one row, and every row is a strict comparison:

| type | two values are equal when |
|---|---|
| `null` | always — one value |
| `bool` | they are the same |
| `int`, `uint`, `float`, `decimal` | mathematically equal across the whole domain: `1 == 1.0` is true, and `decimal` ignores scale, so `1.10 == 1.1000` is true |
| `float` edges | IEEE 754: `NAN == NAN` is **false**, `0.0 == -0.0` is **true** |
| `string` | the same sequence of Unicode scalar values — never numeric, so `"1" == "01"` and `"1e3" == "1000"` are both false, and there is no normalization |
| `bytes` | the same bytes |
| `array<T>` | the same length, the same keys in the same order, and every value equal by this table, recursively |
| class instance | the same object ([`expressions/object-identity-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-object-identity-equality)) |
| enum case | the underlying integers are equal |
| `callable` | the same callable — two anonymous functions with identical bodies are two callables |
| `mixed`, a union | resolved at run time ([`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality)) |

The array recursion terminates: an array is a copy-on-write value rather than a reference, so it
cannot contain itself. An array holding objects compares those by identity, which bounds that walk
too.

The natural ordering used for sorting is a separate question and answers differently for `float`; the
two are not the same table.

<sub>See also [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator), [`expressions/object-identity-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-object-identity-equality), [`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality), [`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused), [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation).</sub>

<a id="expressions-mixed-equality"></a>

## A `mixed` or union operand resolves at run time, and a mismatched pair answers `false`

`rule:expressions/mixed-equality`

`$a == $b` where either side is `mixed` or a union compiles, dispatches on the runtime tags, and
applies [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics)'s table to the row they land in.

**When the two runtime tags belong to different rows, the answer is `false`.** It does not throw, and
it does not convert.

That is the strict answer, not a looser rule returning: a `string` and an `int` are not the same
value. The static case is a compile error rather than `false` for a different reason — there the
compiler can prove the answer before the program runs, which makes it dead code rather than a
question ([`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused)).

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly: **`mixed` is where you pay for not declaring a type.** A
comparison against `mixed` silently answers `false` where a typed one would have refused to compile,
so widening a parameter to `mixed` makes the diagnostic go away without fixing anything.

Nothing here is measured separately: the typed path is one instruction, and the `mixed` path is the
tag dispatch every operation on `mixed` already pays.

**Declined:**
- **A cross-row pair throws**, the way the natural ordering does for a sort or a minimum. Ordering has
  no correct answer for a mismatched pair; equality has one, and it is `false`.

<sub>See also [`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused), [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics), [`expressions/truthy-table`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-table).</sub>

<a id="expressions-object-identity-equality"></a>

## Two objects are equal only when they are the same object, and no class may change that

`rule:expressions/object-identity-equality`

`$a == $b` on two class instances asks whether they are the same object. It never walks properties.

There is **no `__equals`, no `equals()` protocol and no `Equatable` interface**. A per-class equality
hook would make `==` mean something different in every file, and an ambient, undeclared property walk
has unbounded cost in the object graph's size with no way for a class to opt out.

Two named ways to ask the other question already exist:

- **`$a->compareTo($b) == 0`**, where the class implements `Comparable`. A class with a meaningful
  notion of "same value" almost always has a meaningful order too, and this gets both from one
  declaration.
- **`Core\Test::assertEqualsDeep`** in a test, which walks properties, arrays and shapes and produces
  a diff. It is a test member on purpose: a structural walk is a debugging affordance, not something a
  request path should reach for by accident.

A class needing content equality in production and wanting no order writes an ordinary named method.
That reads worse than `==` by exactly one call, and it is visible at the call site. A value class ported
from PHP, whose `==` compared two objects by their properties, pays that call and a `Comparable`
declaration.

**Declined:**
- **Structural equality, PHP's `==` reading.** Its cost is unbounded in the object graph's size, it is
  ambient and undeclarable, and no class can opt out: the same refusal [`classes/comparable`](classes.md#classes-comparable) makes
  for ordering.
- **An `Equatable` interface or an `__equals` hook.** `==` would mean something different per class,
  which is the property removed from every other magic method.
- **A separate identity operator, so `==` could be structural.** That is two equality operators again.
  Identity is the reading a reference type wants by default, and content comparison is the one that
  gains from being visible at the call site.
- **A content-equality member in `Core`.** None exists. One would be a method, never an operator or an
  interface, and the case for it is `compareTo(…) == 0` repeated in real programs.

<sub>See also [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics), [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator), [`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality).</sub>

<a id="expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused"></a>

## Comparing two types that no single value inhabits is a compile error

`rule:expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`

A comparison whose two static types are **disjoint** — no single value inhabits both — is a compile
error (`E0466`), because the compiler already knows the answer and the author did not mean to write
it.

```
string $s = "1";
int $n = 1;
if ($s == $n) { }               // E0466: `string` and `int` are disjoint
if ($s == ($n as string)) { }   // convert once, deliberately, then compare
```

Disjointness, not identity of types, is the test, so ordinary code still compiles: the same type; any
pairing of `int`, `uint`, `float` and `decimal`, which are **one numeric domain**; `?T` against `null`
or against `T`, which is the null test and narrows; a union against any type one member can hold; a
single-value or enum-case type against its base; `mixed` against anything; a class against itself or an
ancestor.

Refused: a non-nullable type against `null`; `string` against `bytes`; an enum against its underlying
integer, where `$e as int` is the written spelling; two unrelated classes; and anything else disjoint.

This turns the entire class of comparisons that could only ever answer one constant into a diagnostic
at the site that wrote it. `$row['id'] == 1` against a string column and `$s == 0` against a
non-numeric string are the common cases.

**Declined:**
- **A statically disjoint comparison answers `false`**, the way a run-time mismatch does
  ([`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality)). The compiler can prove the answer, and code whose answer is
  known before it runs is a mistake worth naming, the same argument definite assignment makes.

<sub>See also [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator), [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics), [`expressions/mixed-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-mixed-equality), [`expressions/switch-match-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-switch-match-equality).</sub>

<a id="expressions-switch-match-equality"></a>

## A `switch` label and a `match` arm compare by the equality rule and by nothing else

`rule:expressions/switch-match-equality`

A `switch` label and a `match` arm are compared against the subject by
[`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics), and by nothing else. There is one comparison in the language,
so there is one here.

A label or arm whose static type is disjoint from the subject's is
[`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused)'s compile error, at the label rather than at the
`switch`.

`match (true) { … }` is unaffected: each arm is a `bool`, tested against `true`.

Truthiness has no part in this. A `switch` subject and a `match` subject are compared, never tested
for truth, and [`expressions/truthy-positions`](expressions.md#expressions-truthy-positions)'s six positions do not include either.

<sub>See also [`expressions/one-equality-operator`](expressions.md#expressions-one-equality-operator), [`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused), [`expressions/equality-semantics`](expressions.md#expressions-equality-semantics).</sub>

<a id="expressions-a-match-has-at-least-one-arm"></a>

## A `match` has at least one arm

`rule:expressions/a-match-has-at-least-one-arm`

A `match` with no arms is `E0476` where it is written. PHP parses one and throws `UnhandledMatchError` on
every evaluation, so no program that ran is lost. A `match` is an expression, and one whose every path
throws has nothing for the position it sits in to bind, pass or return, and no value for a merge with
no incoming edge to carry. A written arm, or `default => throw …`, says the same thing on purpose.

A `match` has one `default` arm at most, and a `switch` one `default:` label. A second one is `E0876`
at its keyword: the first runs for every value no other arm matches, so the second never runs.

For the same reason an arm whose body is a `void` call is `E0868` where it is written, whether the
`match` is a value or a statement: the arm has no value for the merge to carry. A statement per case
is an `if` or a `switch`. A `void` call stored at `mixed` is `E0401`, as it is at any other declared
type, because `mixed` takes every value and a `void` call has none.

<sub>See also [`expressions/switch-match-equality`](expressions.md#expressions-switch-match-equality).</sub>

<a id="expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments"></a>

## A constant argument to an intrinsic `Core` call is validated while checking and prepared into the artifact

`rule:expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`

A short, closed roster of `Core` methods takes an argument that is really a small program — a regex
pattern, a URI, a date format, a duration, a format string, a SQL placeholder list. When that
argument is a compile-time constant, the compiler **validates it while checking** and **prepares**
whatever the runtime call would otherwise derive on first use.

**What crosses to the call is a fact, never an object.** The engine tier a regex pattern settled in,
that a date pattern was written rather than assembled: one word, emitted with the unit as the
member's leading argument. The compiled artifact itself belongs to the core that builds it, which is
what keeps an automaton or a pattern's field list out of a store shared between requests, and it is
what a runtime cache keyed only on what a program *wrote* can then hold for the life of that core.

**A call can also be compiled away.** A `Core\Str::format` template that is a constant, whose
placeholders all read their arguments in order with no flag or width, over types whose text cannot
differ, lowers to the string concatenation it describes, and no call is made. Nothing crosses, so the
bound above holds; `nvs_types::expr_table::FormatPiece` owns which calls qualify.

A malformed constant is a diagnostic pointing at the exact offset inside the string literal. The check on
`Core\Str::format`'s placeholders also counts and types them against the argument list, which turns a
whole family of `printf`-shaped bugs into compile errors.

"Constant" is the existing definition — a literal, a class constant, or an expression over them. No
new notion is introduced, and **nothing is refused for being dynamic**: an argument that does not
qualify compiles to an ordinary runtime call with ordinary runtime validation. The early error, the
static tier report and the preparation are what a constant argument buys, and they are a reason to
prefer it.

This adds no syntax. It is a property of a call whose arguments happen to be constants.

The check exists because an argument of this kind is a program, and a program parsed on first use
fails on whichever path reaches it first — often the error path, often in production. Moving the
failure to check time also makes a security control possible: a regex pattern's engine tier is known
before any request runs, so a deployment can refuse a pattern that can be made to backtrack
([`core-classes/regex-compile-time-tiering`](core-classes.md#core-classes-regex-compile-time-tiering)).

**Declined:**
- **Regex and date literal syntax, such as `/pattern/i`.** `/` is division, and the rules other
  languages use to tell the two apart are a recurring source of parser bugs. The grammar cost is
  permanent, and the benefit over a checked string literal is only how the call looks.
- **Validating every such argument at run time.** It keeps errors that are decidable while compiling
  among the ones found in production, and it leaves a backtracking pattern unrefusable until a request
  reaches it.

<sub>See also [`expressions/intrinsic-list-is-closed`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-list-is-closed), [`expressions/preparation-preserves-behaviour`](expressions.md#expressions-preparation-preserves-behaviour).</sub>

<a id="expressions-intrinsic-list-is-closed"></a>

## The intrinsic roster is a closed set in the compiler's own source, and nothing declares itself into it

`rule:expressions/intrinsic-list-is-closed`

The compiler recognises intrinsics by fully-qualified name from a **closed set in its own source**
(`crates/nvs-types/src/intrinsics.rs`). There is no attribute, no manifest field and no configuration
by which a `Core` class, a subsystem or an extension declares itself intrinsic, and there is no way
for user code to add a row.

Adding an entry is a compiler change with a fixture. Each row names its owner, the grammar its
literal argument is read against, and what preparation produces — so the roster and the validation
that runs over it stay one artefact rather than two lists to keep in step.

A closed set is what makes [`expressions/preparation-preserves-behaviour`](expressions.md#expressions-preparation-preserves-behaviour) enforceable: every row
can be tested against its runtime twin, because the rows are enumerable.

The roster is a permanent coupling between the compiler and the library: the compiler knows a
handful of `Core` method names. The closed set bounds that coupling, since it grows only when a row is
added deliberately. What it costs is that a package or an extension cannot have its own
pattern-shaped argument checked early.

**Declined:**
- **An open intrinsic mechanism**, an attribute or manifest field by which any library declares a
  method foldable. It turns "the compiler knows a few names" into "the compiler runs code a library
  chose while compiling", which is a larger attack surface and much harder to reason about.

<sub>See also [`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments), [`expressions/preparation-preserves-behaviour`](expressions.md#expressions-preparation-preserves-behaviour).</sub>

<a id="expressions-bracket-destructuring"></a>

## `list(...)` does not parse; `[...]` is the only destructuring target

`rule:expressions/bracket-destructuring`

`list(...)` as a destructuring target does not parse. It is `E0230`, naming `[...]`, whose element
grammar is identical in every position — key, nesting depth, skipped slot, reference marker.

```
list(int $a, string $b) = $pair;    // E0230
[int $a, string $b]     = $pair;    // the replacement, identical in every element position
```

The parser still reads the whole construct through to its `;` — the target's elements, the `=` and
the value expression — purely so the diagnostic spans the real statement and recovery resumes cleanly
at the next one. The parsed target is then discarded and the statement becomes an error node: a
rejected construct never reaches the tree as a live node.

`list` stays a reserved word. Freeing it would let a class or a method be named `list`, and keeping it
reserved is what lets the diagnostic fire.

A PHP spelling is reused only when its meaning has no other home in Novis, the test
[`statements/require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct`](statements.md#statements-require-is-the-only-inclusion-construct) applies. `list(...)` fails it: `[...]`
already spells destructuring, and both built the same node from the same element grammar, so no
later stage ever told them apart. With one spelling, the bracket form is the grammar's only entry
into a destructuring statement. The conversion is a bracket for a parenthesis, and every
destructuring leaf already needs a type, so no PHP `list()` site parsed unedited in any case.

**Declined:**
- **`list(...)` kept as a second spelling.** Every argument for it ("PHP programmers know it")
  applies as well to every other refused PHP spelling ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)).
- **`list(...)` kept only for the shape with no keys and no nesting.** A spelling that works for
  `list($a, $b)` but not `list('id' => $id)` is a third rule to teach.
- **Freeing `list` as an identifier at the same time.** That is a reserved-word question with its own
  compatibility surface, unrelated to which destructuring spelling survives.

<sub>See also [`expressions/no-keyword-logical-operators`](expressions.md#expressions-no-keyword-logical-operators).</sub>

<a id="expressions-defaulting-assignment"></a>

## `??+=`, `??-=` and `??.=` are `$a = ($a ?? d) op $v` with the target evaluated once and `d` the zero of the target's type

`rule:expressions/defaulting-assignment`

`$a ??+= $v`, `$a ??-= $v` and `$a ??.= $v` mean `$a = ($a ?? d) op $v`, with `$a` evaluated once and
read the way `??` reads its left operand, so an absent key at any level and a `null` both start from
`d`. That written-out form answers every question about them: which operand types are accepted, what
overflows, what `tainted` and `secret` do, and what the expression's type is. A form that is refused
when written out refuses the operator with the same code.

`d` is the zero of the target's own type: `0` for `int` and `uint`, `0.0` for `float`, the zero
`decimal`, and `""` for `string`. For a `mixed` or union target it is the `int` `0` for `??+=` and
`??-=` and the `string` `""` for `??.=`, and the operator is answered from the runtime tag
([`types/arithmetic`](types.md#types-arithmetic)). A type with no zero, such as a `bool`, an enum or an array, is its own `d`,
so the operator is refused with the codes the plain `+=`, `-=` or `.=` is refused with. A target that
can never be `null` or absent takes the plain `+=`, `-=` or `.=`. The target's declared type is unchanged afterwards and nothing is narrowed ([`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing)).

There are exactly three, and no syntax writes another default: `($a ?? 100) -= 1` is `E0105`, and
`$a = ($a ?? 100) - 1` is that program. `$a ??-1` is a `??` and a `-1`, because each operator ends in
`=`.

They exist because `$counts[$word] += 1` throws on the first word not yet counted, and
`$lines[$day] .= $entry` on the first day, so without them a count, a running total or a grouped string
names its target twice: `$counts[$word] = ($counts[$word] ?? 0) + 1`. That form keeps working, and
neither is preferred. Each operator costs one `null`-or-absent test more than the plain one, with the
same one read and one write of the target; `??.=` copies the accumulated string on each append, as
`.=` on an element or a property does. The default is not visible where the operator is written, and
the default carries neither `tainted` nor `secret`.

**Declined:**

- **Reading an absent target as zero under `+=`, `-=` and `.=`.** A misspelled key would count from
  zero silently, which is the hole [`types/absent-storage-is-never-a-zero-value`](types.md#types-absent-storage-is-never-a-zero-value) closes. These
  operators say where a default is wanted.
- **A default written at the use, `($a ?? 100) -= 1`.** `($primary ?? $backup) += 1` reads as "add to
  whichever exists", so the same syntax would have two meanings.
- **`??*=`, `??/=` and the bitwise forms.** A product or a quotient that starts from zero stays zero.
- **A bare `??+` or `??-`.** `$a ??-1` already means `$a ?? -1`, so each token needs its `=`.

<sub>See also [`types/absent-storage-is-never-a-zero-value`](types.md#types-absent-storage-is-never-a-zero-value), [`types/arithmetic`](types.md#types-arithmetic), [`types/narrowing`](types.md#types-narrowing).</sub>

<a id="expressions-nullable-conversion"></a>

## `expr as ?T` yields the converted value or `null`, and never throws

`rule:expressions/nullable-conversion`

`expr as ?T` produces the value that `expr as T` would produce where that succeeds, and `null` where
it would throw. Every other property of the conversion — what counts as success, the whole-string rule
for `string → int`, the range checks — is the checked form's, unchanged. The operator adds no notion
of validity of its own; it only changes what happens to a failure.

```
var $id   = Core\Request::query('id') as ?uint;      // ?uint — null if absent, or not a uint
var $page = Core\Request::query('page') as ?uint ?? 1;
var $mode = Core\Request::query('mode') as ?SortMode ?? SortMode::Newest;
```

A `null` operand that `as T` rejects yields `null` rather than a diagnostic, which is what keeps the
common shape one line. Where `as T` accepts `null`, `as ?T` gives the same value: `null as string` is
`""`, so `null as ?string` is `""` too. The cost is stated plainly: at such a site an **absent** value and a **malformed** one both
reach the `??`. Where that distinction matters, test the operand for `null` before converting, or use
the throwing form — a value that gates access is converted with plain `as T`.

There is one definition and no family that escapes it: every `as ?T` is the `as T` of the conversion
table, with `null` where it throws ([`expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion-availability)).

The form exists because an absent page number or an unfilled filter is an ordinary outcome, not an
error, and the only other way to reach it is to check and then convert. That parses the same bytes
twice on the request path and needs two definitions of success to agree forever; one operator over
one table is one parse and one definition. `?T` is already the one way to write a value that may be
absent ([`classes/no-undefined-value`](classes.md#classes-no-undefined-value)), so the operator produces an existing type and adds no
syntax: `as` already takes a type, and `?int` is one.

**Declined:**
- **Refusing a nullable operand.** It keeps "missing" and "invalid" apart in the syntax, but it does
  not prevent the conflation: `($raw ?? '') as ?uint ?? 1` collapses the same two states. It would
  only charge a line on the most common shape in the language.
- **A `Core` member per scalar target, such as `Str::toIntOrNull` or `Int::tryParse`.** The name
  shapes are banned ([`core-api/verb-lexicon`](core-api.md#core-api-verb-lexicon)), and it needs one member per target type forever,
  where an operator covers every type, including ones added later.
- **A `Result` or `Either` return that says why a conversion failed.** There is no sum type, and
  adding one to avoid a `null` test is a decision about the whole language.
- **Rewriting PHP's `(int)$x` to `$x as ?int ?? 0`.** It would restore the silent zero that
  [`types/no-legacy-cast`](types.md#types-no-legacy-cast) removes, and it is not even faithful: `(int)"12abc"` is `12` in PHP and
  `null` here. A converter names both forms and lets the author choose.

<sub>See also [`expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion-availability), [`expressions/conversion-keeps-qualifiers`](expressions.md#expressions-conversion-keeps-qualifiers), [`expressions/nullable-condition-lint`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-condition-lint), [`expressions/try-parse`](expressions.md#expressions-try-parse).</sub>

<a id="expressions-nullable-conversion-availability"></a>

## `as ?T` is refused where the conversion cannot fail, where none exists, and at every class target

`rule:expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`

`as ?T` is available for exactly the conversions the checked form already defines, and is a compile
error everywhere else:

| operand → target | `as ?T` |
|---|---|
| any row the conversion table defines | **available**; `null` where the row throws |
| into a single-value or enum-case type | **available** — the non-throwing twin of a checked conversion |
| from `mixed` | **available**; every target has a checked path from `mixed` |
| a conversion that **cannot fail** (`$i as ?int`, `$i as ?string`) | **compile error** (`E0709`), naming `as T` |
| no conversion exists at all (`array<int> as ?int`) | **compile error** (`E0708`) |
| **any** class or interface target | **compile error** (`E0473`), with no exceptions |

Keep the last three rows straight: **a conversion that exists and failed is `null`; a conversion that
does not exist is a diagnostic.** From `mixed` every conversion exists, so `$mixed as ?int` is `null`
for a value holding an array, while a statically-known `array<int>` never compiles. A `?T` that can
never be `null` is a lie in the type and forces a pointless check downstream, which is why the
cannot-fail row is refused rather than allowed as a harmless spelling. A conversion that does not
exist stays a diagnostic because otherwise `as ?T` would be a universal escape hatch that erases
genuine type errors.

**The class row is absolute and admits no roster of blessed names.** `as ?T` spells a downcast in
every language a reader arrives from, and it never spells a parse: text becomes a value through that
class's own reader ([`expressions/try-parse`](expressions.md#expressions-try-parse)).

**Declined:**
- **A roster of class targets that parse, such as `$s as ?Core\Uri`.** It inverts what `as?` means in
  Swift and Kotlin, for a few memorized class names while every other class stays a diagnostic. It
  also removes no spelling: `Core\Uri::parse($s)` exists either way, so the operator only moves the
  parse onto the harder of the two to read.

<sub>See also [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion), [`expressions/try-parse`](expressions.md#expressions-try-parse), [`expressions/disjoint-comparison-refused`](expressions.md#expressions-disjoint-comparison-refused).</sub>

<a id="expressions-conversion-keeps-qualifiers"></a>

## `as ?T` decides `tainted` and `secret` by exactly the rule `as T` uses, and launders nothing of its own

`rule:expressions/conversion-keeps-qualifiers`

Nullability and the security qualifiers are orthogonal axes. `as ?T` runs the **same** qualifier rule
the checked form runs — one code path decides both spellings — so writing `?T` instead of `T` changes
nothing about `tainted` or `secret`.

Where the target is a qualifiable type, the operand's `tainted` and `secret` are carried into the
result: `tainted string as ?string` is `?tainted string`. Where a checked conversion into the target
already launders, `as ?T` launders exactly as much and no more.

**`as ?T` is never a launderer in its own right.** It introduces no qualifier hole the checked form
does not already have, and laundering stays what it is elsewhere: the narrow, sink-named `Core`
members that declare it.

<sub>See also [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion), [`expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion-availability).</sub>

<a id="expressions-try-parse"></a>

## A failable single-`string` parse is spelled `tryParse`, and no separate validity predicate stands beside it

`rule:expressions/try-parse`

A class whose `parse` takes **exactly one `string`** and can fail also carries
`tryParse(string $s): ?T` — `Core\Uri::tryParse` and `Core\Uuid::tryParse` are it today. `tryParse`
**is** `parse` with the throw caught; it is never a second implementation, so there is exactly one
answer to "is this text a `T`".

The global interface `Parses` makes the pair a contract: its one required member is `parse(tainted
string $s): static`, and `tryParse` is a default body on the interface rather than a second required
member. A user class implementing `Parses` declares `parse` alone, and declares its own `tryParse` when
it wants the non-throwing call.

Three conditions keep the shape from regrowing into a `from`/`tryFrom` habit. The `parse` takes one
`string` and nothing else — a parse taking a format or an options bag is a different shape and gets
none. `tryParse` delegates to `parse`. And the spelling is `tryParse`: `…OrNull`, `…Safe` and `…Ex`
stay banned, as does `try…` on every other verb.

**A parse that launders gets no non-throwing twin.** Where laundering is the point, the throw is the
right control flow, and a second launderer to audit is not worth one saved `catch`.

**No separate validity predicate stands beside a parser.** `isValid` members do not exist: a
validity question and its parse answered by two pieces of code is exactly the shape behind
CVE-2024-5458, where one validator accepted user-info that the parser read differently. Ask the
parsed value instead — `Core\Uri::tryParse($s)?->scheme() != null` is the absolute-URI test. A
reader on the parsed value cannot disagree with the parse the way a separate predicate can.

The ban on `try…` names ([`core-api/verb-lexicon`](core-api.md#core-api-verb-lexicon)) admits this one shape because nothing else
reaches it. A `Core` member either throws or returns a `?T` that means absence, and a malformed
string is neither an absence nor something a scalar operator can convert. `tryParse` is not the
scalar `…OrNull` family readmitted: it exists only where `as ?T` does not reach, one member per class
with a failable single-`string` parse.

**Declined:**
- **Making `parse` itself return `?T` and deleting the throwing form.** `?T` would then mean absence
  in one member and failure in another. And the `ParseError` a parse throws lists every offending
  field at once, each located by a dotted path, which a bare `null` discards: that costs little for a
  `Uri` and everything for a CSV or a decoded object ([`core-classes/derive-reports-every-field`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-reports-every-field)).

<sub>See also [`expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion-availability), [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion).</sub>

<a id="expressions-preparation-preserves-behaviour"></a>

## The prepared path and the runtime path are one implementation, so preparation is only earlier and never different

`rule:expressions/preparation-preserves-behaviour`

The prepared path and the runtime path **share one implementation**. The compiler calls the same
pattern compiler, the same URI parser and the same format-plan builder the runtime would have called,
and stores the output. A divergence between the two is a bug of the same class as an incorrect
optimisation, never a permitted difference.

**Preparation is not evaluation.** A call whose result depends on runtime state is not evaluated at
compile time; only the state-independent part is. `$now->format("Y-m-d")` prepares the format plan and
formats at run time, because the instant, the timezone and the calendar are all runtime values. The
narrower case where the whole call is constant folds to its value, but that is ordinary constant
folding.

Because preparation depends only on the literal and on the compiler's own version, it is keyed by the
artifact cache like any other compiled output, including on the compiler-environment component — so a
prepared artifact from a different compiler build is a cache miss rather than a mismatch.

**What preparation stores is a fact about the text, and it reaches the member as an argument.** The
checker files what it prepared under the call's own span, the lowering reads it there and emits it as
a leading constant of that call, and the word rides in the unit's code — so the artifact carries it
with nothing serialized beside it, and a member is handed the answer instead of deriving it again.
The roster of members taking one is closed and lives beside the intrinsic roster, so the slot is a
cost only the members that read it pay; a member on it whose argument was not a literal is handed the
zero word rather than a shorter argument list. The slot is filed under the call and not the literal
because the lowering holds the call's span, and keying on the literal would make it map the written
arguments back to parameters, which only the checker holds the names for
([`core-api/parameters-are-callable-by-name`](core-api.md#core-api-parameters-are-callable-by-name)). The slot is always written because a member's
helper reads one fixed argument list: a constant emitted only where something was prepared would have
it read its first argument from the caller's next slot.

A word the running build does not know is read as "nothing was prepared"
(`crates/nvs-stdlib/src/regex.rs:1288`). Refusing it would turn a compiler-version skew into a failed
request, and the artifact's address already names the compiler build, so a cached unit cannot hand a
process a word another compiler minted.

A **live object is never what crosses**. A compiled pattern belongs to the core that built it, so what
travels for a pattern given as a string literal is the engine tier it settled in and the runtime spends the compile. That
bound is what keeps this rule's first paragraph true across the boundary: the prepared path hands the
runtime path an earlier answer to a question it would have asked itself, never a different
implementation of it.

One observable difference is named rather than denied: a fully folded call is no longer a call, so the
per-call probe does not fire for it. A *prepared* call — the common case — is still a call and probes
normally, and the enclosing statement's probe is unaffected either way.

- **Memory:** one constant per call site on a roster member, and one machine word in the argument list
  of the members that take it. No allocation, no data section and nothing per request; a member off the
  roster is unchanged instruction for instruction.

**Declined:**
- **A table of prepared answers on the compiled program, interned and pointed at.** It is the shape for
  a prepared plan, and the wrong one for a fact that fits in the slot: it buys an indirection and an
  entry per distinct pattern to carry two bits. A fact that needs a table can add one beside this slot.
- **Seeding the per-core pattern cache when a unit loads.** It needs no new argument, but a unit loads
  once and cores are many, so the seeding is either cross-thread or repeated per core, and it only
  pre-fills a cache keyed by text, which not every grammar has.
- **Folding eagerly, evaluating whole calls wherever possible.** The calls worth touching mostly
  depend on runtime state, so an eager rule would either be wrong or need this same carve-out, stated
  less clearly.

<sub>See also [`expressions/intrinsic-constant-arguments`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-constant-arguments), [`expressions/intrinsic-list-is-closed`](expressions.md#expressions-intrinsic-list-is-closed).</sub>

<a id="expressions-pipeline-substitution"></a>

## `|>` substitutes one hole at parse time, and has no run-time representation

`rule:expressions/pipeline-substitution`

`|>` is a binary operator whose right side is an expression containing the hole `$_`. The **parser**
replaces that hole with the left side and emits the resulting expression. There is no run-time
representation of `|>`, and no callable is involved.

```
PipeExpr := Unary ( "|>" PipeRhs )*
PipeRhs  := Postfix                     // a call, an index, a member access, or a parenthesized group
```

`$subject |> RHS` produces `RHS` with its `$_` replaced by `$subject`, left-associative, so
`$a |> f($_) |> g($_)` is `g(f($a))`. The right side is parsed at the postfix level, so an expression
that is not already a call or an access is written parenthesized: `$n |> ($_ * 2)`.

Because the result is the tree the nested spelling produces, every later pass — name resolution, the
type checker, taint and `secret`, literal folding, lowering, codegen — sees a node it already handles.
Nothing about the `Core` roster, scalar methods or any security property changes: `$userTemplate |>
Str::format($_, $n)` is refused for the same reason the nested call is. There is no callable allocated
and no dynamic dispatch.

The operator exists for reading order. A three-deep composition of `Core` calls reads inside-out when
it is nested, and a pipeline reads in the order it runs while every step still names the class it
calls. That class name is what a reviewer reads authority off — `Path::` cannot touch the disk, `IO::`
can — so the composition keeps the signal a fluent method would erase. A hole depends on no
argument-order convention: it reaches any argument slot, an instance method (`$_->group(1)`), an index
(`$_["email"]`), a closure in a variable and `new`. Userland classes need no annotation and no
registration, because the class is written at the call site and resolves the way it always does.

The cost is one more operator on the surface, spent on simplicity of reading, and two ways to write
one composition.

**Declined:**
- **Methods on scalars** (`$s->trim()->upper()`). They erase the class name from the call site, need
  a scalar-to-`Core` map in the type checker instead of a parser rewrite, and collide with `->` on a
  `mixed` receiver, where it already means instance access.
- **A `|>` that applies a callable at run time.** Every step would need `Class::method` as a
  value, and most `Core` methods take a trailing options argument, so they are not unary: nearly every
  step would carry a closure wrapper and read worse than the nesting it replaces. Resolving the right
  side by name at run time is a spelling [`expressions/method-reference`](expressions.md#expressions-method-reference) already closed. The shared
  token's habit is caught by `E0129` ([`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once)).
- **First-argument insertion with no hole.** It cannot reach a second slot
  (`Arr::contains($haystack, $needle)`), it makes a call's arity depend on its context, and userland
  is not bound to put the subject first, so the rule would carry an exception.
- **A different token** — `~>`, `->>`, `==>`. `->>` is one glyph from `->`, `==>` is one from `=>`, and
  `~>` loses the recognition `|>` has across many languages while the lexer would still have to know
  `|>` to catch the habit.
- **A marker attribute that opts a class into fluent calls.** It would make resolution open-world and
  cost the compile-time determinism of name resolution.

<sub>See also [`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once), [`expressions/pipeline-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-precedence), [`expressions/method-reference`](expressions.md#expressions-method-reference).</sub>

<a id="expressions-pipeline-precedence"></a>

## `|>` binds tighter than every binary operator and looser than unary

`rule:expressions/pipeline-precedence`

`|>` binds **tighter than every binary operator and looser than unary**. The four cases that fixes,
each of which a looser placement gets wrong:

| written | groups as |
|---|---|
| `-$a \|> Math::abs($_)` | `Math::abs(-$a)` |
| `"x=" . $a \|> Str::upper($_)` | `"x=" . Str::upper($a)` |
| `$a \|> Str::length($_) > 5` | `Str::length($a) > 5` |
| `$x = $a \|> Str::trim($_)` | `$x = Str::trim($a)` |

Substituting a single hole commutes with the surrounding operator, so `$a |> Str::upper($_) . "!"`
groups as `Str::upper($a) . "!"` and the parenthesis trap a callable-applying pipeline has cannot
arise.

<sub>See also [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution), [`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once), [`expressions/catch-expression-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression-precedence).</sub>

<a id="expressions-pipeline-hole-once"></a>

## The hole is `$_`, it appears exactly once on a right side, and nowhere else at all

`rule:expressions/pipeline-hole-once`

The hole is `$_`. It wears a `$` because it is a binding, and in this language a binding wears a `$`.
The parser turns `$_` into its own node before identifier casing sees a variable, so the rule that
rejects an all-underscore identifier does not fire on it.

**`$_` appears exactly once on a right side** — not at least once. Three refusals keep that
enforceable, and `crates/nvs-diagnostics/src/lib.rs` is the registry that allocates their numbers:

| code | when | what it says |
|---|---|---|
| `E0129` | a right side of `\|>` contains no `$_` | names the shape (`Str::trim($_)`) and, when the right side is a method reference or a callable, adds that this `\|>` substitutes a hole rather than applying a callable |
| `E0130` | `$_` appears more than once on one right side | names binding the value to a local instead |
| `E0131` | `$_` appears anywhere outside the right side of a `\|>` | says the hole has no meaning there |

Exactly one hole is what makes substitution total: no temporary, no double evaluation, and an emitted
tree identical to the nested spelling's. `E0129`'s note on a callable is what makes sharing the token
with PHP affordable: the habit of piping into a callable stops at compile time, at the character where
it goes wrong, and is named.

**Declined:**
- **`$$` as the hole.** `$$name` is the variable-variable syntax, which `E0202` refuses by name, and
  reusing the token for something unrelated is a collision.

<sub>See also [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution), [`expressions/pipeline-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-precedence).</sub>

<a id="expressions-no-null-skipping-pipeline"></a>

## There is no null-skipping pipeline step

`rule:expressions/no-null-skipping-pipeline`

There is no `?|>`. A pipeline step that returns `?T` hands its `null` to the next step like any other
value, so a chain through a nullable result is split with an `if` where the `null` is handled.

A second operator needs a second reason: evidence that a `?T` in the middle of a composition breaks
chains often enough to cost more than the `if` does.

<sub>See also [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution), [`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once).</sub>

<a id="expressions-catch-expression"></a>

## An expression-level `catch` is a chain of typed arms guarding one expression

`rule:expressions/catch-expression`

A `catch` arm is a postfix on an expression. It names one class, optionally binds the thrown object,
and supplies an expression whose value stands in where the guarded expression threw.

```
CatchExpr := Ternary ( "catch" "(" Type Variable? ")" "=>" Ternary )*
```

```
var $cfg = Core\Json::parse($raw) catch (ParseError) => [];
```

The class is mandatory and is one class or interface under `Throwable`, resolved and checked exactly
as a block clause's is — the same codes for a name that is not a class, for a class that is not a
`Throwable`, and for a limit report, which is not catchable here either
([`errors/throwable-hierarchy`](errors.md#errors-throwable-hierarchy)). A union is refused with the block form's own wording: *write two
arms*. The binding is optional and, where written, is a local of the enclosing function under the
block form's rule.

**Arms are clauses of one guard, not guards of each other.** `f() catch (A) => x catch (B) => y` tries
`A` then `B` against what `f()` threw, and `x` is not guarded by the `B` arm. A supertype written
first shadows the arms after it, as in the block form.

The block form is unchanged in every particular and remains the only spelling with `finally`. Resource
cleanup stays there; this form has no one-line twin for it.

**Why the form exists.** A failed conversion, an absent key, every `Core` failure, an arithmetic
overflow and a division by zero all throw, and each costs a caller with a fallback a five-line block.
Definite assignment makes that block dearer than it looks: a local assigned inside `try` is readable
after it only when every `catch` assigns it too, so the declaration, the two assignments and the read
are kept in step by hand. An expression assigns on every path it completes, so the declaration and
the fallback are one line and the checker has nothing to track.

The form sits beside the two value-shaped spellings and does not replace them: `$s as ?int ?? 1` is
the conversion ([`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion)) and `$a["k"] ?? $d` the absent key. `$s as int
catch (…) => null` is legal and pointless, and no diagnostic names it. What a program could catch or
fail to catch does not change: the same landing pad, the same dispatch and the same re-raise run
([`expressions/catch-lowers-to-block-form`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-lowers-to-block-form)).

**Declined:**
- **Extending `??` to swallow any throw.** It is untyped, discards the thrown object and reads as a
  null check. Every reason a conversion throws on garbage would be one `??` away from undone.
- **`try? expr` yielding `?T`.** It is untyped, so it catches everything, and it conflates *threw*
  with *returned `null`*. It is redundant with `as ?T` for the case it does best, and lands every
  result in the nullable-condition trap ([`expressions/nullable-condition-lint`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-condition-lint)).
- **A bare fallback with no `=>`**, as in `f() catch (IOError) 0`. The value dangles after the
  parenthesis with nothing to say it is the result, and `match` already owns the `condition => value`
  syntax a reader knows.
- **A braced multi-arm form**, as in `f() catch { IOError => 0, ParseError $e => throw … }`. Chained
  arms already give several classes, so it would be a second syntax for the same thing.
- **A comma-ok pair** (`v, err := f()`). It needs a tuple return Novis does not have, and costs three
  lines per call.
- **A `Result` type with a `?` operator.** A sum type is a language-scale decision, and it is declined
  for conversions on the same grounds.
- **A `try` keyword opening the guard**, as in `try f() catch …`. The token carries no information:
  the guard starts where the expression does, and an unguarded throw already propagates without one.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-arm-is-an-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-arm-is-an-expression), [`expressions/catch-result-type`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-result-type), [`expressions/catch-expression-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression-precedence), [`expressions/catch-lowers-to-block-form`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-lowers-to-block-form), [`errors/throwable-hierarchy`](errors.md#errors-throwable-hierarchy).</sub>

<a id="expressions-catch-expression-precedence"></a>

## `catch` sits between assignment and the ternary, so one arm guards a whole `??` chain

`rule:expressions/catch-expression-precedence`

`catch` sits **between assignment and the ternary**. The guarded expression is everything the ternary
level parses, so one arm covers a whole `??` chain or a whole `?:`; the arm body is parsed at the same
level, so a following `catch` starts the next arm of the same guard rather than nesting under the
fallback.

| written | groups as |
|---|---|
| `$x = $a / $b catch (ArithmeticError) => 0` | `$x = (($a / $b) catch … => 0)` |
| `$x = $m["k"] ?? f() catch (IOError) => ""` | `$x = (($m["k"] ?? f()) catch … => "")` |
| `f() catch (A) => $y ?: 1 catch (B) => 2` | `f() catch (A) => ($y ?: 1) catch (B) => 2` |
| `f() catch (A $e) => throw new B({previous: $e})` | the `throw` takes everything to its right |

A `throw` arm is therefore written last or parenthesised, and an assignment inside an arm is
parenthesised as it is inside a ternary arm.

Two parses this rules out by construction: `try` never appears in the expression form, because the
guard starts at the expression rather than at a keyword; and a `catch` after an expression can only be
this form, because a block `catch` follows a `}` the statement parser is already inside.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`expressions/catch-arm-is-an-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-arm-is-an-expression), [`expressions/pipeline-precedence`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-precedence).</sub>

<a id="expressions-catch-arm-is-an-expression"></a>

## An arm body is an expression, which admits `throw` and refuses `return` by name

`rule:expressions/catch-arm-is-an-expression`

The arm body is parsed as an expression, and that is the entire rule for what it may hold.

**`throw` is allowed**, because `throw expr` is already an expression. `f() catch (IOError $e) =>
throw new IOError("count failed", {previous: $e})` wraps and rethrows in one line, and the variable on
the left is never assigned — the same answer `$x = $y ?? throw new …` already gives. A `throw` arm is
typed `never` and so contributes nothing to [`expressions/catch-result-type`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-result-type)'s union.

**`return`, `break` and `continue` are refused**, because they are statements. The parser names them
rather than reporting a generic expected-expression: `E0126` — *an arm is an expression; `throw` is
one, `return` is not; for an early return write the block form.*

The refusal is deliberate and not a gap to fill later. A `return null` on an `IOError` hides a
failure, and the block form's five lines are the right price for choosing that.

**Declined:**
- **Admitting `return` in an arm**, as in `catch return err`. The arm would then hold either a value
  or a departure, with nothing in the syntax to say which, and a reader misreads it. The expression
  rule keeps the one departure that is already an expression and refuses the rest by name.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`expressions/catch-result-type`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-result-type), [`expressions/bare-throwable-arm-warns`](expressions.md#expressions-bare-throwable-arm-warns).</sub>

<a id="expressions-catch-result-type"></a>

## The result type is the union of the guard and every arm, and an arm is checked from the pre-guard state

`rule:expressions/catch-result-type`

The expression's type is the union of the guarded expression's type and every arm's, computed by the
same union the `match` arms use. `int $rows = $db->count($q) catch (IOError) => 0;` is `int`; `catch
(IOError) => null` makes it `?int`, and a declaration on the left refuses that with the mismatch
diagnostic it already has. The arm is checked against nothing but the position the whole expression
sits in.

An arm is checked from the **pre-guard** definite-assignment state, as a block clause is: a local the
guarded expression assigned cannot be assumed assigned inside the arm, because the arm runs precisely
when the guard did not complete.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`expressions/catch-arm-is-an-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-arm-is-an-expression), [`expressions/nullable-conversion`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion).</sub>

<a id="expressions-bare-throwable-arm-warns"></a>

## An unbound `catch (Throwable)` arm that supplies a value is warned about

`rule:expressions/bare-throwable-arm-warns`

`W1006` warns on an expression-level arm that names `Throwable`, **binds no variable**, and whose body
is not a `throw`.

In the block form a `catch (Throwable)` has a body with room to log or re-raise. In the expression
form the body *is* the value, so an unbound arm over the root of the exception tree is by construction
*discard every failure, including the ones this site never anticipated* — the suppression operator
this language removed, regrown as a one-liner.

The warning names the two honest spellings: name the class the site expects, or bind `$e` and carry
it. It is a warning rather than an error because the hazard is a habit and not a type error, and
`nvs check` is where habits are named.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-arm-is-an-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-arm-is-an-expression), [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`expressions/nullable-condition-lint`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-condition-lint).</sub>

<a id="expressions-catch-lowers-to-block-form"></a>

## The expression form lowers to the block form's landing pad, with the value in a temporary

`rule:expressions/catch-lowers-to-block-form`

There is no run-time representation of the expression form. It lowers to the block form's lowering —
push the protected region, lower a body, take the thrown reference in the handler block, dispatch by
a chain of class tests, re-raise what no arm matched, join — differing in exactly one way: the body
and each arm produce a value, which is written to one temporary and joined by a phi, the way `match`
joins its arms.

Nothing in the runtime or in codegen changes, and the landing pad is the one already emitted
([`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation)). The cost of a guarded expression that does not throw is the block form's:
zero on the happy path ([`errors/throw-is-not-slower`](errors.md#errors-throw-is-not-slower)).

- **Memory:** nothing. The temporary is the value slot the block form's assignment already needs.

<sub>See also [`expressions/catch-expression`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-expression), [`expressions/catch-result-type`](expressions.md#expressions-catch-result-type), [`errors/propagation`](errors.md#errors-propagation), [`errors/throw-is-not-slower`](errors.md#errors-throw-is-not-slower).</sub>

<a id="expressions-method-reference"></a>

## A method reference is the bare `Class::method` on a class and `$obj->method(...)` on an object, one form per receiver, and a dropped reference is a compile error

`rule:expressions/method-reference`

A method reference takes a reference to a declared method, and each receiver form has exactly one way
to write it. On a class it is the bare member: `Core\Str::length`, `Shop::show`, `self::helper`
(early-bound) and `static::helper` (late-bound), with no `(...)`. On an object it is
`$user->getName(...)`. There is no third form — no `::ref`, and no reuse of `::class`, which stays a
class-name-to-string operator, so one token never means two unrelated things.

**The bare form is unambiguous on a class because the casing rules already separate what `::` can
name.** A constant is `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` (`E0113`), a method is `camelCase` (`E0111`), an enum case
or a nested type is `PascalCase`, and a static property carries `$`. So `Shop::show` can only name a
method. Should the parser be unable to tell a bare reference from a member access before the checker
runs, it produces one node and the checker decides by the casing and the class's members.
`Class::method(...)`, `self::method(...)` and `static::method(...)` do not compile, with a fix that
drops the `(...)`, so a reader meets one form per receiver.

**An object keeps `(...)`**, because a property and a method may share a name and `$obj->name` is the
property. `$obj->method` without `(...)` stays a property read.

**A reference that is created and dropped is a compile error.** `Cache::flush;` as a statement is the
one trap the bare form opens — a forgotten call — and it is refused with a fix to `Cache::flush()`. A
reference written where a `string` or another type that is not `callable` is expected is already a
type error, and its message adds the same hint.

Every form above resolves a method at the reference itself rather than at call time, and the checker
records that resolved target under a variant that cannot be mistaken for an ordinary call. Two shapes
are refused for having no method to resolve: `new C(...)`, because `new` names a class and a method
reference builds a callable carrying a callee rather than an allocation — write `fn (): C => new C(…)`,
which also says which arguments the construction takes; and `$m->method(...)` on a `mixed` receiver,
because a callable outlives the site and there is no class present to read a callee off.

A `callable` may carry its signature. The resolvability this rule is after comes from the reference at
the value's creation site rather than from the static type, so it holds whether or not the slot being
filled declares one.

**Declined:**
- **Keeping `Class::method(...)` beside the bare form.** Two ways to write one reference is surface
  with nothing behind it, and the bare form is the one Java and Kotlin readers already know.
- **Dropping `(...)` on an object too.** `$obj->name` is the property when a property and a method
  share the name, so the bare form would read differently depending on the class's other members.

<sub>See also [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution), [`expressions/nullable-conversion-availability`](expressions.md#expressions-nullable-conversion-availability), [`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values).</sub>

<a id="expressions-no-partial-application"></a>

## Partial function application is not adopted; an anonymous function already spells it

`rule:expressions/no-partial-application`

`f(?, $x)` and every application-with-holes shape do not parse. The value it would produce is
exactly what the callable machinery reduced to one shape ([`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values)), and
an anonymous function already spells every partial application: `fn($a) => f($a, $x)`
([`types/anonymous-function`](types.md#types-anonymous-function)). A second callable-producing spelling, for no capability `fn` lacks,
is what was rejected. Each `?` placeholder is written as a fresh parameter of that wrapper, in order.

The pipeline operator is unaffected: its `$_` is a parse-time substitution, not an application
([`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution)), and the hole diagnostic
([`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once)) already teaches the difference.

<sub>See also [`types/anonymous-function`](types.md#types-anonymous-function), [`types/callable-values`](types.md#types-callable-values), [`expressions/method-reference`](expressions.md#expressions-method-reference), [`expressions/pipeline-substitution`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-substitution), [`expressions/pipeline-hole-once`](expressions.md#expressions-pipeline-hole-once).</sub>
